gloss: “The Divines reckon up several sins as included in this one act of eating the forbidden fruit, namely, pride, uxoriousness, wicked curiosity, infidelity, disobedience, etc.” (Newton).
in the sense ‘that can be accounted for’; not, as more often, ‘liable to render account.’ *to make appear accountable* = to explain, justify.
force = Lat. *momentum*, the metaphor being taken from a balance; cf. “inclining” (46), “even scale” (47).
for the proverb “omittance is no quittance” (i.e. you may leave a thing undone, but not have done with it), cf. *As You Like It*, III. 5. 133.
i.e. has been “scorned.” Man had shown scorn of the gifts of the Almighty by seeking something more which was forbidden him.
M. discusses “The Mediatorial office” of Christ in *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 15.
turned aside. Lat. *derivare*, ‘to divert a stream from its channel,’ hence figuratively, ‘to turn aside, divert.’
proving guilty; this is not necessary because the Serpent has admitted his own guilt by flight.

The whole scene follows Genesis iii. 8–21 closely, the words of the Scripture being worked into the text. In many passages of the poem, especially where he represents the Deity as speaking, M. reproduces the Scripture thus, merely adapting it to the form of blank verse.
in the sense of Lat. *obvius*, ‘coming to meet.’
ever, always.
terms drawn from the stage. ‘It was for you to play the part and character (Lat. *persona*) of ruler.’

because they had an inner application, viz. to Satan, which, for the time, was to be hidden from Adam, who would suppose that they referred to the Serpent. *judged as then best*, an inversion of order; ‘as was then thought best.’

“Here is a manifest indication, that, when Milton wrote this passage, he thought Paradise was chiefly regained at our Saviour’s resurrection” (Bentley). The poet was an old man, and tired, when he set about the second epic, and wisely adapted his choice to his strength.
apparently for the purpose, as hitherto it has been implied that the beasts were not killed by each other or by Adam.

cf. *The Tempest*, I. 2. 250–53, “Thou dost, and think’st it much to tread the ooze of the salt deep” (i.e. a great grievance). *his enemies*; because it was their sin that necessitated His sacrifice.

Addison observes that book X. has a “greater variety of characters” than any other. He compares it with the last act of a tragedy in which all the main *dramatis personae* are introduced and the effect of the action upon them is made clear.

i.e. opposite each other, one “on either side” of the entrance; *vis-à-vis*. Cf. the description in II. 871–89 how Sin, “the Portress of Hell-gate,” opened “the infernal doors” to let Satan pass out on his journey through Chaos to the new-created World and then could not shut them.
i.e. shadow. Sin and Death are always introduced together in the poem: an obvious allegory.
“passing frequently backward and forward; *transmigration*, quitting Hell once for all to inhabit the new creation; they were uncertain which their lot should be” (Richardson).
in the literal sense ‘lean,’ Fr. *maigre*; cf. the conventional representation of Death as a skeleton.

“Of vultures particularly it is said by Pliny, that they will fly three days beforehand to places where there are future carcases. And Lucan has described the ravenous birds that followed the Roman camps, and scented the battle of Pharsalia” (Newton).
shape, form; as commonly in Shakespeare, from the literal meaning ‘make,’ O. Fr. *faiture*, Lat. *factura*. M. purposely uses rather a vague word which leaves much to the imagination.
i.e. the north-east passage, then thought to be practicable and made the object of many voyages of discovery to India and the East.

commonly explained ‘the coast of China’ — with doubtful correctness, however. Formerly, till some time after 1600, the opinion prevailed that ‘Cathay’ was a great region distinct from China, lying north of it and stretching right up to the Arctic Ocean; comprehending, in fact, East Siberia.

one of the Cyclades islands, in the Ægean Sea. “According to a legend, it was called out of the deep by the trident of Poseidon, but was a floating island until Zeus fastened it by adamantine chains to the bottom of the sea.” — *Classical Dictionary*.

i.e. asphalt or bitumen, such as that which floats on the surface of the Dead Sea — thence called ‘Lake Asphaltites.’ Probably Milton here had in mind Genesis xi. 3, where the Hebrew word used for this bituminous substance is rendered ‘slime.’

a Persian city of the province of Susiana and winter residence of the kings of Persia. According to tradition, Susa was founded by Tithonus, the father of Memnon, and Memnon built its acropolis, called after him the Memnonium.

the reference is to the story told by Herodotus (VII. 35), that Xerxes in his anger at the destruction of his first bridge by a storm ordered the Hellespont to receive three hundred lashes from a “scourge” and to have a pair of fetters thrown into it.
literally ‘bridge-making’ (Lat. *pons* + *facere*). It has been suggested that M. used the word with a sarcastic allusion to its other sense ‘belonging to the Pontiff, i.e. the Pope.’

lemma: Betwixt the Centaur and the Scorpion
gloss: “Satan, to avoid being discovered by Uriel regent of the Sun, takes care to keep at as great a distance as possible, and therefore, ‘while the sun rose in Aries,’ he steers his course directly upwards ‘betwixt the Centaur and the Scorpion,’ two constellations which lay in a quite different part of the heavens from Aries” (Newton).
probably meant as a hendiadys = ‘joyful tidings.’

the confines of the Empyrean or Heaven, which M. here treats as a square (“quadrature”) in allusion to the description of the New Jerusalem in Revelation xxi. 16. *orbicular*; the World is always spoken of in the poem as a globe.
an allusion to the formula conferring supreme power on the Consuls at Rome in times of great crisis, namely, *videant consules ne quid respublica detrimenti capiat*.

“Strike” (= ‘to blast’) was the word applied to the evil “influence” which astrologists supposed the planets to exercise on the earth. The belief survives in ‘moon-struck.’ M. says that the planets themselves were ‘blasted’ by bad “influence” as Sin and Death passed near them.

Persian, the ancient Bactria or Bactriana having been a province of the Persian empire. *Sophi*, Shah. *from the horns*, i.e. retreats before the Turkish armies. “During the sixteenth century there was continual warfare between the Persians and the Ottoman Turks” (Keightley).
described in II. 1–4. *state*, canopy.
council. “The Devils are frequently described by metaphors taken from the Turks. Satan is called the ‘Sultan,’ I. 348, as here the council is styled the ‘Divan’” (Newton).
i.e. objecting that Fate did not mean the “secrets” of their realm to be explored thus.
“Milton had no doubt in mind the transformation of Cadmus in the fourth book of the *Metamorphoses*, to which he had alluded before in IX. 506” (Newton); also Dante, *Inferno*, XXIV., XXV. (Todd).

a kind of serpent, supposed to have a head at either end of its body. Sir Thomas Browne has a chapter “Of the amphisbaena” in his *Vulgar Errors*, his conclusion being that “we must crave leave to doubt of this double-headed serpent.”

a serpent whose bite caused great thirst. *the soil*, i.e. Libya in Africa. An allusion to the legend that as Perseus was bringing back the head of Medusa, one of the Gorgons, drops of her blood fell on the soil and caused the country to abound with serpents.
cf. “the dragon” = Satan in Revelation xii. Ovid speaks of the monstrous serpent Python, born from the slime left on the earth by the flood of Deucalion.
one of the Eumenides or Furies, who are described as having serpents twined in their hair.

alluding to the apples of the Dead Sea. Cf. *Eikonoklastes*, 24: “like the apples of Asphaltis, appearing goodly to the sudden eye; but look well upon them, or at least but touch them, and they turn into cinders.”
i.e. over, *once*; emphatic. Man was deceived (by the Serpent) but “once”; the serpents were duped “oft.” *lapsed*; a preterite, I think; ‘fell into error.’

a convenient phrase, under cover of which he can mention theories, yet avoid the responsibility of accepting them. No doubt, M. had some authority for this tradition, but editors have failed to find it.

We must remember that according to the ordinary patristic and mediaeval belief which M. accepted, the fallen Angels became the gods of classical mythology. So M. identifies the Serpent (Satan) with Ophion, one of the Titans and the first ruler of Olympus; and suggests that Eurynome, the wife of Ophion, may have been the same as Eve.
“in allusion to the name Eurynome (= ‘wide-ruling’) he styles Eve ‘the wide-encroaching,’ as extending her rule and dominion farther than she should over her husband, and affecting godhead” (Newton).

M. seems to have had in his thoughts *Julius Caesar*, III. 1. 273, “Cry ‘Havoc,’ and let slip the dogs of war.” The phrase ‘cry “havoc”’ was an old military term for ‘giving no quarter,’ i.e. it was the signal for indiscriminate slaughter.
i.e. by fire, according to 2 Peter iii. 7, 10–13. In *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 33, he treats of “the destruction of the present unclean and polluted world, namely, its final conflagration.”

In *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 13, he says, “All nature is subject to mortality and a curse on account of man”; and that thought is the basis of this long passage dealing with the deterioration in the physical Universe which followed the Fall of Man.

“It is poetically assumed here that, before the Fall, the ecliptic or Sun’s path was in the same plane as the Earth’s equator, and that the present obliquity of the two planes was a modification of the physical Universe for the worse, consequent upon the moral evil introduced by sin” (Masson).

he has previously said that before the Fall only one season was known in Eden, viz. “eternal spring,” IV. 268: a view held by some of the Church Fathers. Classical mythology spoke similarly of the Golden Age.

an allusion to the story of the revenge taken by Atreus, king of Mycenae, on his brother Thyestes: how “Atreus, pretending to be reconciled to Thyestes, recalled him to Mycenae, killed his two sons, and placed their flesh before their father at a banquet.” This spectacle is said to have caused the sun to turn aside.

an obsolete name for a great tract comprehending in modern nomenclature southern Canada and the northern states of America. *the Samoed shore*, i.e. the shore of north-eastern Siberia, near the Gulf of Obi in the Arctic Ocean.

lemma: the Levant and the Ponent winds
gloss: the rising and setting winds, i.e. those which come from the quarters where the sun respectively rises and sets; viz. Eurus, the east wind, and Sirocco, the south-east: Zephyrus, the west wind, and Libecchio, the south-west.
previously (IV. 340–47) the beasts had known neither strife among themselves nor fear of man.

“The wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest,” Isaiah lvii. 20. In *The Reason of Church Government*, II., M. speaks of himself giving up the quiet life of a student, “to embark in a troubled sea of noises and hoarse disputes” (i.e. politics and controversy).

lemma: All that I eat or drink
gloss: “Meat and drink propagate it by prolonging life, and children by carrying it on to posterity” (Newton). William Lauder translated these lines into *quod comedo, poto, gigno, diris subjacet*, and pretended that the Latin occurred in the tragedy of *Adamus Exul* (1601) of the jurist Grotius.
fair (Lat. *aequus*). *reduce*; in the literal sense ‘to bring back’ (Lat. *reducere*), i.e. to the dust of which Adam was made.
Adam should have said “that day.” The time of the action of this book is the day after Adam’s sin.
cf. Horace’s *non omnis moriar*, *Odes* III. 30. 6 (said, however, in a different connection, viz. in reference to the immortality conferred by his poetry).

The spirit, Adam is made to argue, constitutes life and the spirit alone “sinned”: the body is mere “dust,” a “clod,” and as such “properly hath neither” life nor sin: therefore “death,” as the annihilation of life and punishment of sin, must mean the death of the spirit.

“All other agents act in proportion to the reception or capacity of the subject-matter, and not to the utmost extent of their own power” (Newton). So, Adam argues, he cannot be punished after death because death is the utmost punishment that he has the capacity to suffer.
in each of Milton’s drafts of a tragedy on the theme of “Paradise Lost,” Conscience is one of the abstract *dramatis personae*.
Todd shows that this form of invocation is “after the manner of the Italian poets.”
used quibblingly in its literal sense ‘left’ — a reference to the tradition that the rib out of which Eve was fashioned was taken from Adam’s left side — and also in the figurative sense ‘unlucky.’

The passage is like a commentary on the proverbial line, “The course of true love never did run smooth,” *A Midsummer-Night’s Dream*, I. 1. 134. That M. when he wrote the lines was thinking of the circumstances of his own first marriage cannot be doubted.

a personal allusion appears to be intended. Edward Phillips, the poet’s nephew and one of his biographers, states that after Milton’s first wife refused to live with him he paid much attention to a Miss Davis; so that “too late” represented his own experience.
in her grief she, like Adam, forgets the words of their Judge which clearly showed that “the instant stroke of death” was “removed far off” (210, 211).
Probably Milton’s reconciliation with his own wife was present to his thoughts; cf. *S. A.* 1003–1007.
at “the place” where their Judge appeared to them and pronounced their sentence; or perhaps he means ‘in Heaven.’
considering that we are in such evils; Lat. *ut*.
‘Though we have the power, through choosing the quickest of the many ways of dying, to destroy destruction (i.e. Death’s future work of destroying mankind) by destroying ourselves.’
struggling.
he means that the curse applied more to the ground than to himself; so he says quibblingly that it ‘glanced’ off him and ‘fell to the ground,’ e.g. like an arrow that just grazes the object aimed at.
kindle. *thwart*, flashing across the sky. Probably he alludes to one of the theories as to the origin of fire on earth which Lucretius gives, viz. that it came through the thunderbolt and lightning.
For a similar instance of repetition (a figure imitated from the classics) cf. IV. 641–56. It is curious that the next book begins “Thus they, in lowliest plight, repentant stood Praying.”
